acquisition_note: Public full-text books, articles, and preprints acquired from author, publisher, institutional, or arXiv locations and extracted locally with mutool. The scratchpad is git-ignored. Hashes identify the acquired PDFs and complete extracted text files. Source acquisition is not itself evidence of reading; completed relevant units and limits are recorded per source.

sources.title: The Elements of Statistical Learning: Data Mining, Inference, and Prediction, Second Edition, Corrected 12th Printing
sources.publication: Springer Series in Statistics, 2017 corrected printing
sources.read_status: complete relevant units read; the complete 764-page book was not read cover to cover
complete_relevant_units_read: Chapter 3, §§3.2–3.9, printed pp. 43–100: least squares, ridge, Lasso, LARS, PLS/PCR, group lasso, pathwise optimization; Gauss–Markov proof is assigned as an exercise.

Chapter 4, §§4.1–4.5, printed pp. 101–135: indicator regression, Gaussian LDA/QDA, regularized discriminants, logistic likelihood/IRLS, L1 logistic, perceptron and separable hyperplanes; perceptron convergence proof is Exercise 4.6.
§5.8, printed pp. 167–173: RKHS representation, finite-sample representer form, squared-loss kernel regression; representer proof is cited/assigned to an exercise.

Chapter 8 §8.5, printed pp. 272–281: EM for a mixture example, general EM formulation and likelihood monotonicity explanation; assumptions and proof references are not a general parameter-convergence theorem.
Chapter 9 §9.2, printed pp. 305–316: CART regression/classification trees and cost-complexity pruning.
Chapter 10 §§10.1–10.12, printed pp. 337–365: AdaBoost/exponential loss, boosting trees, gradient boosting, shrinkage and subsampling.
Chapter 12 §§12.2–12.4, printed pp. 417–438: hard/soft support-vector classifiers, dual/KKT and kernel methods.
Chapter 13 §§13.2.1–13.2.3, printed pp. 460–463: K-means prototypes, LVQ and Gaussian mixtures as soft prototypes.
Chapter 14 §§14.3.4–14.3.7, printed pp. 507–512: combinatorial clustering, K-means descent and Gaussian mixtures/soft responsibilities.
Chapter 14 §14.5.1, printed pp. 534–541: empirical PCA projection and SVD formulation.
Chapter 14 §§14.5.3–14.5.5, printed pp. 544–552: spectral clustering, kernel PCA and sparse PCA.
Chapter 14 §14.6, printed pp. 553–554: nonnegative matrix factorization and nonuniqueness.
Chapter 14 §§14.7.1–14.7.2, printed pp. 558–565: latent-variable/factor analysis and ICA assumptions/identifiability discussion.
Chapter 14 §§14.8–14.9, printed pp. 570–576: metric/classical MDS, ISOMAP, LLE and local MDS.
Chapter 15 §§15.1–15.4.3, printed pp. 587–602: random forest definition, OOB, variable importance, overfitting discussion, variance/decorrelation and bias.
Chapter 17 §§17.2–17.4.4, printed pp. 627–645: Markov graphs, Gaussian precision models, graphical lasso, discrete Ising models, hidden nodes and RBMs.
Chapter 18 §18.4, printed pp. 661–667: L1/elastic-net linear classification and fused Lasso.
Chapter 18 §18.5.2, printed pp. 670–672: inner-product kernels and pairwise-distance conversions.
limitations_and_open_proof_notes: This is a methods-oriented textbook; many claims are given without proof or assigned to exercises. In particular, Gauss–Markov, perceptron finite convergence, general representer statements, the Gaussian precision/conditional-independence equivalence, Hammersley–Clifford, and manifold-recovery guarantees are not all proved in the cited units.
§5.8 states the general representer form but cites Wahba/exercises; do not treat that as a local proof.
§14.5.3 presents spectral algorithms and graph energy identities but leaves consistency/perturbation results to cited literature.
§14.6 assigns the NMF auxiliary-function derivation as an exercise and notes nonuniqueness.
§14.7 explains ICA identifiability conditions but does not prove the theorem.
Empirical benchmark performance and tuning recommendations are not distribution-free generalization guarantees.

sources.title: Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning
sources.read_status: complete relevant units read; the complete 266-page book was not read cover to cover
complete_relevant_units_read: Chapter 2, §§2.1–2.8, printed pp. 7–30: Bayesian linear regression, GP regression, Gaussian conditioning formulas, marginal likelihood and exact computation.
Chapter 4, §§4.1–4.4, printed pp. 79–102: covariance kernels, PSD Gram matrices, stationary kernels, Bochner and Mercer theorem statements, kernel constructions and smoothness examples.
Chapter 6, §§6.1–6.4, printed pp. 129–150: RKHS, regularization, representer result, SVM primal/dual and MAP/regularization comparison.
limitations_and_open_proof_notes: Finite-dimensional GP posterior formulas are stated and derived from Gaussian conditioning; they do not establish path continuity.
Bochner and Mercer theorem proofs are referred to external sources; Mercer is presented under finite-measure/continuity assumptions.
Moore–Aronszajn and the general representer theorem are stated with references rather than fully proved here.
The exact GP cubic-time cost is a finite dense linear-algebra statement; numerical conditioning and finite precision remain relevant.
Non-Gaussian GP classification uses approximations; it is not covered by the exact Gaussian regression posterior.

sources.title: The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy
sources.publication: Foundations and Trends in Theoretical Computer Science 9(3–4), 2014
sources.read_status: complete relevant chapters and proofs read; full book acquired/extracted
complete_relevant_units_read: Chapter 2, printed pp. 11–27: neighboring databases, (ε,δ)-DP, postprocessing, group privacy and limitations.
Chapter 3, printed pp. 28–65: sensitivity, Laplace, exponential mechanism, composition, advanced composition and sparse vector, including complete relevant theorem proofs.
Chapter 11 §§11.1–11.2, printed pp. 216–230: finite-class private ERM/PAC sample calculation and differentially private online learning, including theorem proofs through Theorem 11.6.
limitations_and_open_proof_notes: State database adjacency and whether it is add/remove or substitution; constants differ.
The finite-class private ERM range can be computationally enormous, so the result is information-theoretic rather than generally efficient.
The book's basic private-learning exposition is not a client-level federated privacy theorem.
Floating-point implementations of ideal continuous-noise mechanisms require careful numerical treatment.

sources.title: Estimating High-Dimensional Directed Acyclic Graphs with the PC-Algorithm
sources.read_status: complete relevant article and proof appendix read
complete_relevant_units_read: Sections 2–4, printed pp. 613–620: DAG/CPDAG setup, PC skeleton and orientation procedure, sample partial-correlation tests and assumptions.
Theorems 1–2 and Appendix A, printed pp. 628–636: uniform skeleton and CPDAG consistency proofs.
limitations_and_open_proof_notes: Consistency assumes Gaussianity, faithfulness, causal sufficiency, polynomial p growth, sparse maximum degree and a minimum partial-correlation separation rate.
Gaussian conditional independence iff zero partial correlation and the Markov-equivalence characterization are cited standard results; local proof suppliers are still needed.
The CPDAG identifies an equivalence class and does not orient every edge.

sources.title: Causal Discovery with Continuous Additive Noise Models
sources.read_status: complete relevant definitions, theorem statements, algorithms and proofs read
complete_relevant_units_read: Section 2, printed pp. 2014–2020: continuous additive-noise model and identifiability setup.
Section 3.1 and Theorem 20, printed pp. 2021–2023: bivariate identifiability condition.
Sections 3.2–3.3, Theorems 28 and 34, printed pp. 2024–2029: restricted multivariate identifiability and RESIT.
Appendix A.5, A.11–A.15 and associated proof text, printed pp. 2040–2049.
limitations_and_open_proof_notes: Identifiability depends on continuous positive densities, additive independent noises, causal minimality and the stated differential-equation/restricted-ANM conditions.
RESIT's correctness theorem is population-level and assumes consistent regression plus a perfect independence oracle.
The finite-sample HSIC/regression implementation is not covered by a broad high-dimensional consistency theorem.

sources.read_status: complete mathematical method, SDP formulation and solver appendix read; unrelated benchmark-result passages not treated as theorem evidence
complete_relevant_units_read: Sections 2.1–2.3, printed pp. 209–215: Mahalanobis metrics and prior metric-learning methods.
Sections 3.1–3.5, printed pp. 216–221: target neighbors, impostors, hinge loss, convex PSD reformulation and energy classifier.

Experimental test-error improvements do not give a generalization guarantee.

sources.title: Random Forests
sources.read_status: complete article text read; proof appendices read
complete_relevant_units_read: Sections 1–4, printed pp. 1–9: infinite-forest vote limit, margin, strength/correlation bound and random-feature forests.
Section 11, printed pp. 24–26: regression-forest results and unbiasedness condition.
Appendices I–II, printed pp. 29–33: proofs of Theorem 1.2 and strength/correlation bound.
limitations_and_open_proof_notes: The classification limit is conditional on fixed training data and iid tree randomizations; it is not a monotonic finite-B risk theorem.
The regression result assumes E_Y Y=E_X h(X,Θ) for every randomized tree.
Theoretical parameters are population quantities; practical OOB estimates are estimates, not exact identities.

sources.title: A Tutorial on Spectral Clustering
complete_relevant_units_read: Sections 2–5, full tutorial, printed/preprint pp. 4–22: unnormalized/normalized Laplacians, spectral algorithms, RatioCut/NormalizedCut relaxations, random-walk connection, perturbation discussion and limitations.
limitations_and_open_proof_notes: The tutorial states Davis–Kahan and points elsewhere for its proof.
No general approximation guarantee follows from spectral relaxation; the tutorial gives counterexamples and emphasizes graph/parameter dependence.
Manifold-Laplacian convergence results are cited rather than proved.

sources.title: Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data
sources.publication: AISTATS 2017, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 54
sources.read_status: complete algorithm/setup/conclusion units read; paper is empirical rather than a convergence proof
complete_relevant_units_read: Sections 1–4, including Algorithm 1, global/local objective definitions, non-IID/unbalanced client setup and experiments.
limitations_and_open_proof_notes: The paper explicitly emphasizes empirical evaluation and does not prove a general convergence theorem for FedAvg.
Keeping raw data on devices is not a formal differential-privacy guarantee; updates may leak information.
The paper's fixed-client synchronous experimental setup omits multiple deployment complications.

sources.title: SCAFFOLD: Stochastic Controlled Averaging for Federated Learning
sources.read_status: complete algorithm, theorem assumptions and relevant convergence proofs read
complete_relevant_units_read: Sections 2–5, Algorithms 1–2 and Theorems I–III: objective, FedAvg/SCAFFOLD updates and rates.
Appendix B assumptions A1–A5; Appendix D.2 FedAvg proof; Appendix E.1–E.2 SCAFFOLD convex and nonconvex proof routes.
Theorem IV is quadratic-only and was read with that restriction.
limitations_and_open_proof_notes: FedAvg's theorem uses bounded gradient dissimilarity; retain the stated smoothness, variance and convexity assumptions.
SCAFFOLD theorem rates depend on client sampling, local steps and specified step sizes; do not quote a rate without those conditions.
Theorem IV's local-step result is for quadratic client functions and cannot be generalized to arbitrary smooth functions.

sources.title: Local SGD Converges Fast and Communicates Little
complete_relevant_units_read: Sections 1–3, Algorithm 1, Theorem 2.2 and Corollary 2.3: local SGD and strongly-convex smooth convergence.
Appendix A proof of Theorem 2.2 and Appendix B asynchronous local-SGD proof; nonconvex results are explicitly outside this paper's guarantee.
limitations_and_open_proof_notes: The theorem assumes L-smooth and μ-strongly convex global objective, bounded stochastic-gradient variance and second moment, prescribed decreasing stepsize and synchronization gap.
Communication-gap scaling is an asymptotic condition; one-shot SGD is not covered by the stated guarantee.
The authors explicitly do not provide a guarantee for the general nonconvex setting in this paper.

sources.title: Sharp Thresholds for High-Dimensional and Noisy Recovery of Sparsity
sources.publication: UC Berkeley Technical Report, May 2006; arXiv:math/0605740v1
sources.read_status: complete paper and main theorem proof read
complete_relevant_units_read: Sections 2.2–2.3, printed pp. 5–7: deterministic-design mutual-incoherence result and proof.
Sections 3.1–3.4, printed pp. 8–15: random Gaussian ensemble assumptions, Theorem 1, threshold corollaries and complete success/failure proof.
limitations_and_open_proof_notes: The theorem concerns exact signed/support-pattern recovery, not generic prediction risk.
It assumes Gaussian design/noise, mutual incoherence, eigenvalue bounds, beta-min scaling and asymptotic growth of s, n−s and p−s.
General covariance ensembles have upper/lower threshold constants that need not coincide; the exact sharp constant 1 is for the identity-covariance Gaussian ensemble.

sources.title: Sparse Inverse Covariance Estimation with the Lasso
complete_relevant_units_read: Sections 1–5, printed pp. 1–9: Gaussian sparse inverse-covariance objective, blockwise lasso equivalence, coordinate algorithm and empirical examples.
limitations_and_open_proof_notes: This paper describes an optimization algorithm but does not give a full global convergence proof for its implementation.
The result is for Gaussian observations and estimates an undirected conditional-dependence graph; it does not identify causal direction.
Penalty scaling and whether diagonal precision entries are penalized must be specified.
